items.title: Bank of America hit with $1.2bn fine for money laundering failings
items.summary: Bank of America has been fined $1.2 billion by the US Treasury for failing to detect money laundering and violating sanctions. The bank admitted to willfully violating the Bank Secrecy Act by neglecting its reporting and due diligence obligations.

brief.what: The US Treasury Department fined Bank of America $1.2 billion for systemic failures in its anti-money laundering and sanctions compliance programs. The bank failed to report over $5 billion in suspicious transactions, including those linked to national security risks, and admitted to willfully violating the Bank Secrecy Act.
brief.who: Bank of America is the primary actor, while the US Treasury Department, the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC), and the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) acted as the regulators.
brief.context: The fine is the third-largest ever imposed by the Treasury. The bank relied on external inquiries rather than internal controls to detect illicit activity, effectively outsourcing its reporting obligations.
brief.why: Regulators stated the bank failed to maintain compliant anti-money laundering programs and conduct due diligence on foreign accounts. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent noted that these failures exposed the entire US financial system to significant illicit finance risks.
brief.next: Bank of America stated it is committed to addressing the regulatory issues and will include the $1.2 billion charge in its third-quarter earnings results.

items.title: What an economics Nobel Prize winner knows about pricing
items.author: Erika Ryan
items.summary: Robert Hall and Michael Woodford have been awarded the Nobel Prize in Economics for their research on stabilizing economic cycles. Their work emphasizes how forward-looking expectations and clear communication from policymakers influence business pricing decisions.

also.author: Eshe Nelson
also.title: Robert E. Hall and Michael Woodford Awarded Nobel for Economics

also.title: A Nobel prize for how to keep economies on an even keel
also.note: The Economist frames the award around the practical application of keeping economies stable.

also.author: Graeme Wearden
also.title: Nobel Prize for economics awarded to Hall and Woodford for work on ‘smoothing’ crises
also.note: The Guardian highlights the specific focus of their work on 'smoothing' economic crises.

brief.what: Stanford's Robert Hall and Columbia's Michael Woodford were awarded the Nobel Prize in Economics for their research into macroeconomic stability. Their work explores how microeconomic behaviors, specifically how businesses set prices and how individuals make purchasing decisions, drive broader economic cycles.
brief.who: Robert Hall and Michael Woodford are the Nobel laureates; Michael Woodford is a professor at Columbia University.
brief.context: The research focuses on the 'boom and bust' cycles of the economy and the importance of forward-looking expectations in pricing. It highlights that businesses do not just react to current costs but adjust prices based on their predictions of future economic conditions.
brief.why: Woodford argues that policymakers must communicate clearly and predictably to manage public expectations. He suggests that when policymakers fail to provide such guidance, it can lead to economic instability and public uncertainty regarding affordability.

items.title: No, Giving Immigrants Research Jobs Is Not Fraud​
items.author: Josh Pauzé
items.summary: Vice President J.D. Vance has launched a probe into nine elite universities over their use of J-1 visas for federally funded research. The administration alleges these institutions are exploiting the program to undercut American wages, though critics argue the investigation lacks evidence of actual fraud.

brief.what: Vice President J.D. Vance and Labor Department Inspector General Anthony D'Esposito have initiated an investigation into nine universities, including Harvard and MIT, regarding the use of J-1 visas for federally funded research. Officials claim these schools use foreign labor to avoid employment obligations and undercut American researchers, citing that 61 percent of researchers at these institutions are foreign nationals compared to 38 percent elsewhere.
brief.who: Vice President J.D. Vance and Labor Department Inspector General Anthony D'Esposito are leading the probe, targeting elite research universities.
brief.context: The J-1 visa is an exchange program that does not require employers to pay prevailing wages or Social Security taxes, unlike the H-1B visa designed for high-skilled foreign workers. This investigation follows a history of Trump administration efforts to restrict foreign worker programs and exert federal influence over higher education.
brief.why: Vance argues the universities are using the program to exploit taxpayer-funded grants and displace American workers. The article suggests the move is part of a broader protectionist agenda and an attempt to exert federal control over academic institutions.
